I'm a little concerned about introducing Meson options to override the defaults defined in PDI. My understanding is that, if defaults are defined in PDI, they are part of the interface contract, then allowing each consumer to change them at build time means the documented behavior and the implementation can diverge.


If the defaults are actually intended to be platform-specific, then perhaps they shouldn't be defined in PDI in the first place and should instead come from a platform configuration layer ? 

The reason that we made them false by default is because , SPDM policies can alter the security model of the system & redfish model seems to show that an external verifier does the verification of the measurement values (hence an external agent who is responsible for verification also would set the policy as well). https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/phosphor-dbus-interfaces/+/85393/comment/04e261c4_832c6f7a/ documents the reasons for the default a bit more elaborately.

Can you comment a bit more on "why" we are need this overriding capability in the daemon ?

>if defaults are defined in PDI, they are part of the interface contract.

I agree that we should not have defined these default values in the PDI because they are platform-specific configurations.


For example, one platform may require only a specific subset of PQC algorithms, another may support only SPDM 1.1 or only SPDM 1.2, while another platform may require secure session establishment. These are all platform-specific policy decisions and should not be dictated by the PDI.

>The reason that we made them false by default is because , SPDM policies can alter the security model of the system & redfish model seems to show that an external verifier does the verification of the measurement values

Yes, It can and it should be up to the platform owner what the securtiy plicy should be.

I agree that SPDM policies can affect the security model. However, the security policy should be determined by the platform owner, not by the PDI.

From my perspective, it is also inconsistent to claim that SPDM is provided as a distro feature while SPDM communication is disabled by default. These default values should not have been defined in the PDI in the first place, as they introduce unnecessary assumptions and create confusion.


The daemon needs the ability to override these settings because the appropriate SPDM configuration depends on the target platform and its security policy, not on the generic interface.

Different platforms have different requirements—for example, supported PQC algorithms, SPDM version (1.1 vs. 1.2), whether secure sessions are mandatory, or whether certain SPDM features should be enabled. These decisions are driven by platform capabilities, compliance requirements, and the overall security model.

If the PDI defines fixed defaults, those defaults effectively become part of the interface contract and may not be suitable for every platform. Allowing the daemon to override these values enables platform owners or integrators to apply the correct policy without changing the interface itself. This keeps the PDI platform-agnostic while allowing each deployment to enforce its intended security policy.

Why not run time configuration for the default security settings.

1. Manufacturing Process Is Not Atomic or Guaranteed
Manufacturing steps can fail, be skipped, If the Redfish API call to set policy properties is missed (tooling bug, network issue, rushed line), the device ships with the hardcoded PDI defaults silently. Compile-time defaults give the platform/vendor a safety net - the right behavior for 
their product is baked in at build time and doesn't depend on the manufacturing workflow executing perfectly.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
2. Different Products Need Different Defaults Without Runtime Setup
A security focused product (e.g. one that must enforce verify-certificate=true, spdm enabled = true, version = x.x, supported algorithms) can ship a binary where that is the default without requiring manufacturing to configure it. The compile-time option is an ODM/OEM customization point — different customers building different images can have different starting points, without touching runtime workflows at all.

3. Air-Gapped deployments                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              
Some deployments never have a Redfish client talking to them at manufacturing. Embedded use cases, or stripped-down deployments may not run the Redfish configuration step at all. Compile-time defaults handle these without needing any runtime intervention.

4. Manufacturing Time
say millions of boards even a 1–2 second Redfish API call per board adds up fast:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      1 million boards × 2 seconds = 555 hours of pure API execution time 

5. hidden costs per board on the line
Error handling and retry logic if the call fails
Verification call afterward to confirm the property was actually set

I see that this commit https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/spdm/+/92060 has already been merged. If spdmd is started with a state directory, for example:

spdmd --state-dir /path/to/your/dir

and a policy.json file is placed in /path/to/your/dir, PolicyManager::load() will read it during startup and populate all the SPDM policy properties from it.

The JSON format is:

{
  "Version": 1.1,
  "Enabled": true,
  "SecureSessionEnabled": false,
  "VerifyCertificate": true,
  "AllowExtendedAlgorithms": false,
  "AllowedVersions": ["ALL"],
  "AllowedAlgorithmsAEAD": ["ALL"],
  "AllowedAlgorithmsBaseHash": ["ALL"],
  "AllowedAlgorithmsBaseAsym": ["ALL"]
}

Given this, it seems we no longer need this commit, as we already have a mechanism to configure these settings based on platform requirements.

I would like the defaults to be some kind of sane defaults.  I don't understand why "enabled=false" is a good default for us.  Shouldn't we make the default "widely useful and available"?

My general feeling is that people should not have to "provision" a system to make it do something expected.  Having to do provisioning means that after a factory reset (or file system corruption) the system is now in an undesired state.

Thanks, Patrick. Agreed enabled=false as the default is a poor choice.
The intent was to allow platforms to set their own defaults at build time via Meson options, but the option defaults themselves should be widely useful. I'll change the default for enabled to true (and revisit the others) so the system works
out of the box without provisioning. Does that address your concern?
Yes.  Let's change the PDI default values to something meaningful.  That will automatically create the default policy with those values.

Choices seems better option, so that we can identify any errors during compilation itself.

choices: ['ALL', 'NONE', '1.1'],
Also later once we add 1.2, 1.3 support same can be updated here to indicate the same.

convertStringToSpecialSetValues is a sdbusplus-generated function that already handles "ALL" and "NONE" (they are the valid enum string representations). The else if branches are dead code — they can never be reached. If convertStringToSpecialSetValues fails on "ALL", the fallback will succeed, masking a real upstream bug
